issues.legal_issue: The statutory restriction limiting a protected tenant’s ejectment to specified grounds applies to a pre-enactment ejectment suit that is pending when the tenant-protection amendments take effect.
material_facts: The ejectment suit was filed before the original tenant-protection Act came into force and remained pending through appeals when the amendments took effect.
The amendments brought the defendant within the statutory definition of a protected tenant.
The landlord did not establish any of the specified grounds for ejectment.
issues.conclusion: The tenant could rely on the statutory restriction in the pre-enactment suit, and ejectment was unavailable because the landlord proved none of the permitted grounds.
issues.legal_principle: Although statutes are generally not construed retrospectively to defeat vested rights, retrospective operation may follow from express language or necessary implication. The overriding language of section 3—making a protected tenant liable to ejectment only on specified grounds and not otherwise—showed that the restriction applied to pending pre-enactment suits. The Court referred to the general principles in Craies on Statute Law and Halsbury’s Laws of England, and to Knight v. Lee and Beadling v. Goll on retrospective operation and pending claims.

rule.if: pre_act_ejectment_suit and case_pending_when_tenant_protection_amendment_took_effect and tenant_covered_by_amended_definition and not permitted_eviction_ground_proved

predicates.pre_act_ejectment_suit: A landlord began an ejectment suit before the tenant-protection law came into force.
predicates.case_pending_when_tenant_protection_amen: The suit or an appeal in it was still pending when the relevant tenant-protection amendment took effect.
predicates.tenant_covered_by_amended_definition: The defendant fell within the protected-tenant definition as amended.
predicates.permitted_eviction_ground_proved: The landlord proved at trial at least one ground on which the law permitted the protected tenant to be ejected.

issues.definition: When a pre-enactment ejectment suit remains pending after the amendment and the defendant is covered by the amended definition, the landlord cannot obtain ejectment without proving a permitted ground.

issues.legal_issue: The statutory notice and application requirements for initiating post-enactment ejectment proceedings do not apply to a pre-enactment ejectment suit.
material_facts: The landlord filed the ejectment suit before the tenant-protection Act came into force.
The suit continued in the civil courts after the Act and its amendments took effect.
The landlord had not initiated the suit by giving the notice or applying to the Controller contemplated by the Act.
issues.conclusion: The majority held that the notice requirement in section 4 and the Controller-application requirement in section 5 were prospective and did not invalidate the pre-enactment suit.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4 and 5 were framed for a landlord wishing to initiate ejectment after the Act came into force: section 4 required notice, and section 5 required an application to the Controller. Their language and the former transfer provisions, sections 28 and 29, showed that those requirements were prospective. Justice Bhargava expressly reserved his opinion on section 4; the majority view was that it was prospective.

predicates.pre_act_ejectment_suit: A landlord began an ejectment suit before the tenant-protection law came into force.
predicates.civil_court_proceeding_continued_after_t: The pre-enactment suit continued in a civil court after the tenant-protection law took effect.

issues.definition: A pre-enactment ejectment suit that continues in a civil court is not subject to the notice and Controller-application requirements for initiating a new proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: Omission of the provisions for transferring pending suits and proceedings to the Controller does not make a pending pre-enactment ejectment suit infructuous or remove the civil court’s jurisdiction to decide it.
material_facts: The ejectment suit was filed before the tenant-protection Act came into force and continued through civil-court proceedings and appeals.
The 1953 amendment omitted the provisions that had provided for transfer of pending suits and proceedings to the Controller.
The defendant came within the protected-tenant definition, so the civil court had to consider the statutory restriction on ejectment.
issues.conclusion: The civil court retained the duty to decide the suit under the provisions applicable to it, including the restriction limiting ejectment to specified grounds; the suit did not become infructuous merely because the transfer provisions were omitted.
issues.legal_principle: After sections 28 and 29 were omitted, no provision remained for transferring the pending suit to the Controller. Sections 4 and 5 did not apply to a pre-enactment suit, but section 3 did. The civil court therefore had to decide the suit by applying section 3. The Court discussed Mahadeolal Kanodia v. Administrator-General of West Bengal in connection with the effect of omitting section 28.

rule.if: pre_act_ejectment_proceeding and transfer_provisions_omitted and no_transfer_mechanism_available and tenant_protection_rule_applies

predicates.pre_act_ejectment_proceeding: A civil-court ejectment suit or appeal began before the tenant-protection law came into force.
predicates.transfer_provisions_omitted: The provisions that had directed transfer of pending proceedings to a specialist decision-maker were removed.
predicates.no_transfer_mechanism_available: No remaining law provided for transferring the pending proceeding to that decision-maker.
predicates.tenant_protection_rule_applies: The defendant is covered by a tenant-protection rule governing the grounds for ejectment.

issues.definition: When a pending pre-enactment ejectment proceeding has no available transfer mechanism, the civil court must decide it under the applicable ejectment rules rather than treat it as infructuous.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord need not state a permitted eviction ground in the notice of ejectment, but must prove a permitted ground at trial where ejectment is restricted to specified grounds.
material_facts: The notice of ejectment did not state any of the grounds specified by the tenant-protection law.
The landlord made no attempt to establish any specified ground at trial.
The defendant was treated as a protected tenant under the amended definition.
issues.conclusion: The omission of a permitted ground from the notice did not itself prevent the landlord from proving one at trial, but ejectment was properly denied because no permitted ground was proved.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 restricted ejectment to the specified grounds but did not require those grounds to be stated in the notice. The existence of a permitted ground could be proved at trial. The separate notice requirement in section 4 was prospective and did not apply to this pre-enactment suit.

rule.if: ground_limited_ejectment_proceeding and eviction_ground_omitted_from_notice and not permitted_eviction_ground_proved

predicates.ground_limited_ejectment_proceeding: The proceeding concerns a tenant whose ejectment is permitted only on specified grounds.
predicates.eviction_ground_omitted_from_notice: The landlord’s notice did not state a specified ground for eviction.
predicates.permitted_eviction_ground_proved: The landlord proved at trial at least one ground on which the law permitted ejectment.

issues.definition: In a proceeding limiting ejectment to specified grounds, omitting a ground from the notice does not itself bar the claim, but failure to prove a permitted ground requires denial of ejectment.
